content:
"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles. 'In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,' Cavanagh found. 'It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.'

The glaring oversight in police protocol left a trail of missed opportunities to prevent a tragedy, culminating in the death of Dale Scott Walkinshaw. On the night of September 16th, officers stumbled upon a scene they would never forget. As they drove through the quiet streets of Darwin, their routine patrol was interrupted when they spotted the aftermath of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux lay crumpled against a once-proud palm tree at the intersection of Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport.

The officers' attention was quickly drawn to a shadowy figure moving amidst the nearby vegetation. Emerging from behind the cover of leaves, Dale Scott Walkinshaw held an injured woman in his arms. The woman, a recent acquaintance from a local bar, slipped in and out of consciousness as the pain from her back injury became overwhelming.

Though Walkinshaw remained physically unscathed by the accident, the emotional toll of the night’s events weighed heavily on him. The smell of alcohol lingered in the air, later confirmed by a roadside test showing he was well over the limit with a reading of 0.149.

As the officers began to assess the situation, the true extent of the dire predicament became apparent. The jagged timeline of ignored warnings and delayed implementations painted a grim picture of systemic negligence. Yet, at that moment, all that mattered was the wellbeing of those they had sworn to protect and serve.

Tragically, the system had failed Walkinshaw, much like the many others who showed vulnerable signs before him. The absence of crucial safeguards, warned about in reports from years past, loomed like a specter over the unfolding events. In their hearts, the officers knew this was more than just an accident. It was a rallying cry for change, echoing a sentiment that would demand accountability and reform in the days to come.

Cavanagh’s findings served as a somber reminder that the cost of inaction is not only measured in lives lost but also in the shattered trust of a community yearning for justice."
